source.title_on_document: Writing, creativity, and artificial intelligence. ChatGPT in the university context

supplement.where: None. The paper mentions no supplementary material, appendix, posted data, or code. A text search of all 10 PDF pages finds none, and the only OSF link is a reference entry (PDF p. 10).
supplement.holds: Nothing outside this PDF. The descriptives are in Tables 2 and 3 (PDF p. 6, journal p. 50) and the contrast statistics in Tables 4 and 5 (PDF p. 7, journal p. 51). No table prints n or standard errors.

paper_design_summary: Two designs. First, the researchers gave Games 2 (uses of a rubber tube) and 3 (what would happen if people never stopped growing) of the Spanish PIC-A creative imagination test to 20 free or freemium text-generation AI systems and to university students working without aid (193 analyzed, at three Spanish universities), and compared fluency, flexibility, and narrative originality with Mann-Whitney U tests. Second, in the same one-hour session, the students repeated both games with ChatGPT, told to improve their first answers, and the paper compares pretest and posttest scores with Wilcoxon tests in a one-group pretest-posttest design with no control group and no random assignment.

studies.label: AI systems versus unaided students on PIC-A Games 2 and 3 (descriptive, ex post facto comparison)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned. The scores of 20 AI systems are compared with the unaided (pretest) scores of 193 students.
assignment.quote: a descriptive and comparative non-experimental or ex post-facto quantitative research study was carried out, in which the level of creativity achieved by both the AI systems and the students was analysed

ai_tool.name_model: 20 systems (Table 1): ChatGPT, Copy.ai, Rytr, Peppertype, Copysmith, Jasper, Writesonic, Youchat, Anyword, ASKtoAI, Contentbot, Copymatic, Dupla, Magic Write (Canva), Neuro-Flash, Nichesss, ReAI, Simplified, Unbounce, Wordtune. All with OpenAI/GPT-3 technology except Dupla.ai.

task.description: PIC-A (Creative Imagination Test for Adults, Artola et al. 2012). Game 2: list all the things a rubber tube could be used for (alternate uses). Game 3: imagine what would happen if people never stopped growing (consequences).
task.duration: Students: 10 minutes per game per the manual. AI systems: no time limit; the same instruction sent three times in a row.

eligibility.reason: No study randomly assigns people to AI. S1 compares the output of 20 AI systems with the students' unaided output, and no person receives AI help (ai_vs_human). S2 is a one-group pretest-posttest: the students did the games first without aid and then with ChatGPT, in a fixed order within one one-hour session per group, with no control group (quasi_people, which the codebook places in observational context). The word 'random' appears nowhere in the paper. The paper-level class is observational because S2 is the only study in which people work with AI and the only one whose outcomes answer an atlas question (with_ai). S1 stays ai_vs_human at the study level. Criterion 2: 193 students analyzed, far above 50. The paper states 193 participants and describes no exclusions. The tables print no n, but the Table 4 U and Z values fit 193 students against 20 systems, and every Table 5 effect size equals |Z|/sqrt(193) (arithmetic checks, not stated in the paper). Criterion 3: the PIC-A scores are computed from the written answers with the manual's correction instructions.

one_line_finding: In a one-group pre-post design with no control group (193 students analyzed at three Spanish universities), scores after the students revised their PIC-A answers with ChatGPT were higher on Game 2 fluency (10.47 to 13.08), flexibility (7.56 to 8.33), and narrative originality (11.02 to 14.45), all p <= .002, and on Game 3 fluency (9.52 to 10.05, p = .025); separately, 20 AI systems outscored the unaided students on Game 2 but not on Game 3 (PDF p. 7, Tables 4 and 5).
open_questions: Whether one-group pretest-posttest designs (quasi_people) appear on the site as observational context or only in the screening report (codebook Section 13). If only in the report, the paper's on-site context reduces to S1's ai_vs_human comparison.
The posttest is a revision of each student's pretest answers, and there is no unaided second-attempt group, so AI help and a second attempt at the same items are confounded.
Tables 3 to 5 print no n, and the paper does not say whether all 193 students completed the posttest.
Each AI system received each instruction three times. The paper does not say whether a system's score pools, averages, or selects among the three responses.
Who scored the student and AI answers, and whether scorers knew the phase or the source, is not stated.

differences.a: observational (A chose it because S2 is the study with people using AI, and flagged the choice as an open question)
differences.resolved: observational. The paper holds two context designs, and the field takes one value. S2 is a one-group pretest-posttest in which the same students work first without AI and then with ChatGPT under no random assignment. Codebook Section 3 places this in observational context ('Comparisons of people who work with and without AI under non-random assignment also go here'). S2 is also the only study in which people work with AI and the only one whose outcomes answer an atlas question (with_ai). S1's outcomes answer none. The abstract states the aim as AI 'as a support for the teaching-learning process'. S1 keeps design_class ai_vs_human at the study level, so no information is lost. This matches the reconciled forms for non-random comparisons of people (c056, c074, c114: observational). If Review 1 decides that before-and-after designs appear only in the screening report (codebook Section 13), the paper's on-site context reduces to S1's ai_vs_human comparison.
differences.quote: Secondly, a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest study was carried out, where the creativity indicators obtained by the students, both before and after a learning intervention with the help of ChatGPT, were evaluated and compared.
differences.locator: PDF p. 4 (journal p. 48), Section 2.1 Design; PDF p. 1 (journal p. 45), Abstract

differences.b: output (B's note: one scored response set per AI system or per student for each game)
differences.resolved: participant. Each observation in the Mann-Whitney comparison is one respondent's PIC-A direct score for a game: one per student (Table 3 gives student minima and maxima) and one per AI system (Section 3 lists per-system direct scores). Each score aggregates all of that respondent's answers, so it is not a single idea or story, which is what the codebook calls an output. The same student scores are the S2 pretest scores, which both forms code as participant. On the AI side the observation is one AI system, not a person, and measure_detail says so.

reconciliation.notes: Non-substantive differences were harmonized without counting them: arm names and description wording; the S2 'delay' field (A empty, B 'Posttest in the same one-hour session'), where both mean no delay, so the final leaves it empty and keeps the session fact in task.duration; and the wording of the one-line finding, notes, and open questions, which are merged. The markdown omits Tables 1 to 5 as pictures, so every table value was read from zoomed renders of the PDF. A's note said the Results text attributes the manual means (15.54 and so on) to the AI systems ambiguously. The sentence attaches those values to the manual, and the final notes say so.

open_items.item: On-site display of one-group pretest-posttest designs (open question 1, and the context_class choice that reconciliation difference 1 resolved as observational). Codebook Section 13 leaves it to Review 1 whether non-randomized before-and-after comparisons appear as observational context or only in the screening report. If only in the report, the paper's on-site context reduces to S1's ai_vs_human comparison. The answer changes the context class, not any of the three criteria: criterion 1 fails either way.

AI help is confounded with a second attempt at the same items (open question 2). Every student revised the pretest answers with ChatGPT, and no group made an unaided second attempt (PDF p. 5, Section 2.4). The paper describes this procedure in full. It limits what the S2 contrast can show, but it changes no criterion: criterion 1 fails because nothing was randomized and there is no comparison group.

Number of students in the posttest (open question 3). Tables 3 to 5 print no n, and the paper does not say whether all 193 students completed the posttest. The arithmetic fits 193: the Table 4 U and Z values fit 193 students against 20 systems, and every Table 5 effect size equals |Z|/sqrt(193). Criterion 2 would fail only if fewer than 50 students completed both phases, and nothing in the paper suggests it. Core is no under any count, because criterion 1 fails. The exact count matters for extraction (n per arm), not for eligibility.

How each AI system's three responses per game enter its score: pooled, averaged, or one selected (open question 4). It concerns only the S1 AI-versus-human context comparison, in which no person receives AI help, and affects no criterion.

Who scored the student and AI answers, and whether the scorers knew the phase or the source (open question 5). Criterion 3 holds because the PIC-A scores are computed from the written answers with the manual's correction instructions (PDF p. 5, Sections 2.4 and 2.5). The scorers' identity and blinding bear on the quality of the measure, not on the criterion.
